statement: In young people in the United States in the 1960s, sudden deaths right after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons (solvents and aerosol sprays), without suffocation in a plastic bag, were described in a series of 110 deaths gathered by a nationwide survey in 1969 whose methods are not described (Bass, 1970). Those who died were aged 11 to 23, and 37 were known to have sniffed before, occasionally or habitually; the products were mostly aerosol propellants (fluorocarbons; 59 deaths) and the cleaning solvent 1,1,1-trichloroethane (29), then toluene (8), benzene (7) and gasoline (4) (editors' sums of the paper's map); the report lists no alkyl nitrite (poppers). Where an autopsy is described, it found no anatomical cause of death; volatile hydrocarbons were found in the organs in 44 deaths (how many were tested is not given), so a positive toxicological result is not reported for most of the series; how the remaining cases were classified is not stated. In six eyewitness accounts the person suddenly ran, screamed or became agitated, or called out that his heart was stopping, just before collapsing; eight people dashed a few hundred feet and then collapsed; and an activity or stress, such as being surprised by parents or police, running from police, wrestling or riding a bicycle, was listed for 18 deaths. Family or friends hid the sniffing in 8 deaths. Products considered of low toxicity on the basis of human and animal experiments were among those involved. The author proposed that the hydrocarbons make the heart prone to a sudden fatal rhythm, intensified by raised carbon dioxide or by adrenaline from fright or exertion, drawing on cat and anaesthesia studies; no heart rhythm was recorded in any death, and he wrote that it is difficult to say what caused the terminal event accompanied by panic. With no count of how many people sniffed, the series cannot say how often sniffing ends in sudden death or whether this was becoming more common (the abstract's 'sharp rise' in incidence has no rate behind it), and without sniffing episodes that did not end in death to compare with, it cannot show that fright or exertion raises the risk. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In the United States in the 1960s, 110 young people aged 11 to 23 died suddenly right after sniffing solvents or aerosol sprays, mostly spray propellants or a cleaning solvent; the report did not list poppers. Where an autopsy was described, it found no other cause of death, and several people suddenly ran or panicked just before they collapsed. The author proposed that the chemicals upset the heart's rhythm, with stress, effort or a build-up of carbon dioxide adding to this. No heart trace was recorded; this was a proposed explanation from other studies. The survey counted deaths, not how many people sniffed, so it cannot say how often this happens.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_bass_1970, JBI checklist, high: deaths gathered by an undescribed survey, with no case definition or attribution criteria; toxicology reported positive in 44 of 110 with the number tested unknown; circumstances recorded for few deaths; no comparison group.

indirectness.note: Worded for the series' place, period and products; it is not applied to poppers (alkyl nitrites), which the report does not list.

imprecision.note: No estimate is given; counts only.

grade.reasoning: A case series without a comparison starts low; rated down for risk of bias: very low. The claim describes the deaths that were recorded, as the paper allows; it gives no rate, trend or risk factor, and the heart-rhythm explanation is reported as the author's proposal from animal and anaesthesia studies, not as a finding. The counts are a minimum: the survey's completeness is unknown, and concealment means that some deaths after sniffing were probably not recognized. The claim covers solvents and aerosol sprays only. Later death series (for example Darke et al., 2023, on the reading list) were not read. Status single study.

statement: Among 116 adults in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once, surveyed in 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (Allott & Redman, 2006; 51 in 100 women, mean age 26.5), every respondent reported at least one thing they did to avoid ecstasy's negative side effects, chosen from a list: most often drinking water (96 in 100), limiting the amount of ecstasy (71 in 100), taking breaks or chilling out (62 in 100), a healthy lifestyle (60 in 100) and vitamins or natural products (53 in 100); 30 in 100 took other illegal drugs and 16 in 100 prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown (the acute recovery period), 4 in 100 had no strategy, and to avoid brain damage, 18 in 100 had none. 41 in 100 had taken pharmaceuticals or natural products before ecstasy ('preloading') and 47 in 100 after it ('postloading'): among those who listed them, half took multivitamins and 41 in 100 took 5-HTP (a building block of serotonin) before, followed by magnesium and fruit or juice, and 46 in 100 took 5-HTP and 44 in 100 multivitamins after; among those who gave reasons, 46 in 100 did it to ease the comedown, 33 in 100 to reduce brain damage and 22 in 100 to seek more pleasure (55 respondents could give more than one reason). These are reported motives, not evidence that a product had those effects. About 39 in 100 had ever tested their pills (61 in 100 never had; editors' calculation), and 53 in 100 had changed how they used ecstasy because of something they disliked about it, most of them by using it less often. Every respondent had also used at least one other substance with ecstasy, most often alcohol (91 in 100 before and 81 in 100 during use) and amphetamines (60 in 100 before and 66 in 100 during). Preloading and postloading were more common among respondents who had used ecstasy more than 50 times (preloading 55 against 30 in 100), among at least 30 focal tests without correction, with other comparisons also reported. These figures describe one self-selected sample, not how common the practices are: respondents found through harm-reduction websites may be more interested in harm reduction, the response rate is unknown, validation or piloting of the questionnaire is not reported, and the article gives no reference period or use frequency for the prompted Table 4 strategies; pill-testing and preloading/postloading frequencies were asked. Whether any of these practices lowers harm was not studied: the authors note that the evidence that preloading protects comes only from studies in rodents, most given injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRI antidepressants or St John's wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome, which this survey did not examine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 2004 survey of 116 people in Australia who had used ecstasy, almost all said they drank water to avoid side effects, and most said they limited how much they took or took breaks. About 4 in 10 had taken vitamins, 5-HTP or other products before ecstasy, and about half afterwards; the most common stated reason was easing the comedown, while about one in five of those giving reasons sought more pleasure; about 4 in 10 had ever tested their pills. This was a self-selected group, so its numbers do not show how common these habits are. Whether any of them lowers harm was not studied, and the authors warn that 5-HTP and some antidepressants taken with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_allott_2006, JBI prevalence checklist, high: no sampling frame; acquaintances, their networks and self-selected readers of two harm-reduction websites; unknown response rate; questionnaire validation/piloting not reported; prompted strategy list with no reference period specified in the article; denominators vary from 101 to 116.

indirectness.note: One Australian sample in 2004; the practices and products people use may differ in other places and years, and Table 4 strategy frequency/reference period is not given, although pill-testing and preloading/postloading frequencies were asked.

imprecision.note: 116 respondents: shares near 40 to 50 in 100 have 95% intervals of about ±9 points (editors' calculation); product/reason subsets rest on 46 to 55 people and have wider intervals, about±12–14 points for shares near half (editors' Wilson calculations).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low; rated down for risk of bias (a self-selected sample likely to over-represent interest in harm reduction) and indirectness: very low. The claim gives what this sample reported, not population prevalence, and says nothing about whether any practice works, which the paper did not study. Section 7, findings only, held for the senior author: products are named as respondents reported them, with the authors' caution about serotonin syndrome, and no amounts or timings are given. The 21.8% reporting a pleasure-related motive is included only as a survey finding about reasons, without linking it to particular products, amounts, timing or demonstrated effects. The paper calls itself the first study of these practices, but its own introduction describes an earlier UK survey (Akram & Galt, 1999), not read. Later surveys of preloading (Copeland et al., 2006; Kelly, 2009) and the rat studies behind it (Sprague et al., 1994) are on the reading list and were not read. Status single study.
